body_markdown:
*Almost every global capability center plan to own outcomes end to end. Very few have made the shift. Here is why centers stall, and a scorecard to find out where yours stands.*


**Short answer:** GCCs have become very good at doing the work. Today they build products, shape data and AI strategy, and drive enterprise-wide change. The next step is owning outcomes, and that means more than moving additional roles offshore or adding AI, engineering, or analytics capabilities. Ownership starts when a GCC can make decisions, control an outcome, and be measured on the business result. Most centers aren’t there yet.


Now, while most centers deliver strongly on cost, some experience cost inflation of 7-10% year on year. While it’s still significantly lower than onshore, it’s become a problem that GCCs are trying to solve. Few get there, because the way centers are measured, funded and given decisions keeps them focused on cost. The GCC Value Scorecard below shows where your center creates value today, and where to start.
Where plans meet reality


Read any GCC survey from the past year and the ambition is clear. In[EY’s 2025 GCC Pulse Survey](https://www.ey.com/en_in/newsroom/2025/11/58-percent-gccs-in-india-investing-in-agentic-ai-two-third-creating-dedicated-innovation-teams-to-globalize-ideas-ey-gcc-pulse-survey-2025) , 87% of India centers said they plan to manage end-to-end processes for their global business within 12 months. 58% are investing in agentic AI. Two thirds are building dedicated innovation teams.


Now look at the results.[BCG’s 2025 research](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2025/india-rewriting-the-global-capability-center-playbook) found that only 8% of GCCs have advanced significantly across innovation, competitive differentiation, and efficiency. Most remain focused on delivery.[HFS’s 2026 reference](https://www.hfsresearch.com/research/hfs-horizons-global-capability-centers-gcc-services-2026/) checks with enterprise GCC leaders show the same pattern from another angle: service partners score well on cost, reliability and talent, and have yet to deliver strong AI-led productivity and innovation.


While ambition is close to universal, shifts are rare. Most GCCs sit somewhere between, and that is where the next few years of value will be decided. A center that stays in delivery gets compared with a vendor quote at every budget cycle. A center that owns outcomes becomes part of how the company competes.


## Where GCC Value Builds


GCCs began as offshore centers set up to save money.[Today they are expected to build products, shape data and AI strategy, and drive enterprise-wide change](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/case-studies/construction-firm-delivers-8-products-with-gcc/) . The value builds over time: it starts with cost and control, then grows into capability, innovation, and growth. Each step asks something different of the center and headquarters.


**Saving money still matters.** It funds everything else, and it earns the center the trust to take on more. It becomes a problem only when it is the one thing the center is asked to do.


**Building products is where ownership starts.** The center stops receiving specifications and starts making decisions on architecture, priorities, and trade-offs. One useful question for GCC leaders is, therefore: what important decision can your center make today without asking headquarters for permission? If the answer is difficult to identify, moving additional work to the center won’t solve the problem, but moving decision rights might.


**Owning data and AI is the area most centers say they are working on.**[BCG found](https://yourstory.com/enterprise-story/2025/06/gccs-yet-to-make-their-mark-on-innovation-index) that over 90% of top-performing GCCs run advanced AI use cases, against about half of the rest. What separates them is ownership: someone in the center is accountable for a use case reaching production and moving a number the business tracks.


**Driving enterprise-wide change is the rarest, and the most valuable.** Here, the center helps decide how the company works: which processes to redesign, where to automate, and which capabilities to build next. This is starting to open up.[EY found](https://www.ey.com/en_in/newsroom/2025/11/58-percent-gccs-in-india-investing-in-agentic-ai-two-third-creating-dedicated-innovation-teams-to-globalize-ideas-ey-gcc-pulse-survey-2025) that 52% of India centers now share accountability for global decisions. The other 48% are consulted at most.


## Why Centers Stall


Talent is rarely a blocker anymore. Attrition at India GCCs fell from 13% in 2023 to 9% in 2025, and 81% of centers are upskilling their teams on GenAI ([EY](https://www.ey.com/en_in/newsroom/2025/11/58-percent-gccs-in-india-investing-in-agentic-ai-two-third-creating-dedicated-innovation-teams-to-globalize-ideas-ey-gcc-pulse-survey-2025) ).[Nasscom and Zinnov](https://cxotoday.com/others/from-delivery-engines-to-ai-nerve-centers-indias-gccs-take-the-global-lead/) found that 64% of site leaders also hold a global functional role. The people are ready. What holds most centers back is what those people are allowed to own. A few sticking points explain most of the gap.


- **The current scorecard only measures cost.** A center reviewed on cost and service levels gets very good at cost and service levels. If the business wants products or AI results from its GCC, those outcomes need to be on the scorecard, with targets, and reviewed with the same weight.
- **Decisions are made somewhere else.** Work arrives as tickets and specifications. The center’s leader hears about the roadmap after it is set. In EY’s survey, 26% of India centers are formally consulted on global decisions, and 22% have no formal role at all.
- **AI stays in pilots.**[Nasscom research](https://research.agilebrandguide.com/reports/nasscom/beyond-arbitrage-forging-strategic-partnerships-with-next-gen-global-capability-centers-gccs) found that 95% of GCC leaders say their companies get no measurable impact from AI pilots. Pilots stall for familiar reasons: the data sits behind a request to headquarters; nobody in the center owns production, and success was never defined as a number.
- **The budget only funds delivery.** A center funded as an annual cost line has little room to build skills, platforms or leadership ahead of the work. A center expected to build products needs that investment first, so it is ready when the work arrives


.


## The GCC Value Scorecard


## Read your total


Then look at your scores by area. The area with the lowest score is usually where to start, even when your total looks healthy. A center can look mature overall while still having almost no decision authority. Another may possess excellent engineering capability but no production of AI ownership.


The scorecard is designed to expose those gaps.


.


## What To Do Next, By Stage


Two principles apply at every stage. Move one area at a time: One fully owned product is worth more than five partially owned products. One AI solution in production is worth more than ten pilots. One genuine enterprise decision right is worth more than multiple advisory committees. And change the scorecard before you change the work, because the center will deliver what it is measured on.


## Five Questions for Your Next Leadership Review


1. What outcomes does our GCC genuinely own today?
2. Where does our center create value today, and where will we need it in two years?
3. What does our scorecard reward?
4. Which decisions could the center own next year?
5. Which AI pilot will reach production this year, and who in the center owns it?
6. What are we funding beyond delivery?


## Where To Start


The scorecard gives you a quick read. Our GCC Maturity Assessment goes further:


It evaluates cost, location and talent; operational, technology and AI readiness; economics and transition readiness; and risk. The output is a recommended operating model, prioritized capability roadmap, business case, and implementation path. It can be used whether a GCC is currently operated internally or with a partner.


The principle behind it is straightforward:


Don’t begin by asking how much more work can move to the GCC. Begin by asking what the GCC should own.
For organizations that are not ready for a full assessment, a Discovery Call can provide a starting point to map priorities and identify where the biggest ownership opportunity sits.
